title: Keep it Coherent: A Meta-Analysis of the Seductive Details Effect https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-020-09522-4 https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-keep-it-coherent-a-meta-analysis-of-the-seductive-details-effect/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page summarises Sundararajan and Adesope's meta-analysis of 68 studies on the 'seductive details effect' -- the tendency of interesting but irrelevant information (an amusing anecdote, an eye-catching but off-topic image) to hinder rather than help learning. The overall finding is a negative effect on learning, but the size of that effect varies with the type and presentation format of the seductive detail, the design of the surrounding materials, and methodological features of the underlying studies. Static seductive details such as images proved more harmful than dynamic ones such as animations, seemingly because students try to connect static images to the content and end up overloaded. The effect was also worse when seductive details appeared in both text and image form, and worse on paper than in digital formats that let students segment and revisit material. Notably, the authors found seductive details were most damaging in science and social science content but potentially beneficial in mathematics, where they may help offset math anxiety. Barton highlights the bottom-line recommendation: minimize seductive details in instructional materials, especially where recall (rather than recognition) is being tested.
points: Seductive details reliably harm learning across 68 studies, but the size of the harm depends heavily on format and subject.
Static seductive details like images are more damaging than dynamic ones like animations, likely because students try to integrate images into their understanding.
Seductive details combined in both text and image form, or presented on paper rather than digitally, cause the most harm.
Seductive details may actually help in mathematics, potentially by reducing math anxiety, even as they hurt learning in science and social science content.
Open-ended recall questions are more sensitive to the negative effects of seductive details than multiple-choice questions are.
